dissolution-free-energy-s1.title: Dissolving four salts
dissolution-free-energy-s1.text: Standard enthalpy and entropy of solution for four ionic solids in water. Assume the values do not change with temperature.

table.caption: ΔH°soln and ΔS°soln for four salts

dissolution-free-energy-s2.title: Ions in water
dissolution-free-energy-s2.text: A student draws one cation (M⁺) and one anion (X⁻) surrounded by water molecules after a salt dissolves. In each water molecule the oxygen end is partly negative and the hydrogen ends are partly positive.
dissolution-free-energy-s2.html: Key: dark circle with label, an ion; mid-size orange circle, oxygen atom; small white circle, hydrogen atom.

items.q: Calculate ΔG°soln for NH₄NO₃ at 298 K.

mistakes.why: Value: convert ΔS° to 0.1087 kJ/(mol·K) before multiplying by T.
Value: T must be in kelvin, 298 K, not 25.

why.correct: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° = 25.7 − (298)(0.1087) = 25.7 − 32.39 = -6.7 kJ/mol. The subtraction leaves the tenths place, so −6.7 kJ/mol (two significant figures).

items.q: NH₄NO₃ dissolves readily in water and the water gets colder. Which statement explains both observations?
options: The ions release energy as water molecules surround them, which makes ΔH° negative and ΔG° negative.
ΔH°soln > 0, so the water cools, but the ions spreading out makes TΔS° > ΔH°.
The water gets colder because ΔS° is negative, and a negative ΔS° makes ΔG° negative.
Dissolving is a physical change, so ΔG° does not apply and the salt dissolves because it is ionic.

why.correct: Endothermic (the water cools) but entropy-driven: TΔS° = 32.4 kJ/mol outweighs ΔH° = 25.7 kJ/mol.
options: If ΔH° were negative, the water would warm up. The cooling shows ΔH° > 0.
Right: ΔH°soln > 0 (the water cools), yet ΔG°soln < 0 because the entropy term wins.
ΔS° is positive here, and a negative ΔS° would make ΔG° less negative, not more.
ΔG° applies to physical changes too. Many ionic solids barely dissolve.

items.q: Which salt’s dissolving is favored mainly because of the enthalpy change, even though the entropy change works against it?
options: NH₄NO₃
NaCl
Salt Z
CaCl₂

why.correct: CaCl₂: ΔG° = −81.3 − 298(−0.0447) = −68.0 kJ/mol. The enthalpy term drives it.
options: Its ΔH° is positive (unfavorable); it dissolves because of the entropy term.
Both ΔH° (+3.9) and the entropy term matter, but ΔH° is unfavorable here.
Its ΔG° is positive at 298 K, so its dissolving is not favored.
Right: ΔH° = −81.3 kJ/mol is strongly favorable and outweighs the unfavorable −TΔS° = +13.3 kJ/mol.

items.q: Salt Z has small, doubly charged ions. Which explanation of its negative ΔS°soln is best?
options: Each small, highly charged ion holds water tightly; that water’s lost freedom outweighs the ions’ spreading.
The ions of Salt Z stay in the crystal, so they do not disperse through the water.
The solution is more disordered than the solid, which makes ΔS° negative.
Dissolving Salt Z releases heat, and releasing heat lowers the entropy of the solution.

why.correct: Two effects compete: ions dispersing (S up) and water held in hydration shells (S down). For small, highly charged ions the second wins.
options: Right: strong ion-dipole attractions order the water; that loss of microstates is larger than the ions’ gain.
Some Z does dissolve; the ions that dissolve do spread out. The water ordering is what makes ΔS° negative.
This argument would give a positive sign, and "disorder" is not a particle-level reason.
ΔH° and ΔS° are separate quantities; the cause here is the ordering of water around the ions.

items.q: Calculate ΔG°soln for Salt Z at 298 K.

mistakes.why: Sign: ΔS° is negative, so −TΔS° = −(298)(−0.1200) = +35.8 kJ/mol.

why.correct: ΔG° = −9.0 − (298)(−0.1200) = −9.0 + 35.76 = 26.8 kJ/mol. Positive, so Salt Z is only slightly soluble (Ksp = e^(−ΔG°/RT) is about 2 × 10⁻⁵).

items.q: Is the orientation of the water molecules in the drawing correct?
options: No: the oxygen should face the anion, because both are electron-rich.
No: the hydrogens should face the cation, because hydrogen bonds form to cations.
Yes: δ− oxygen faces the cation and a δ+ hydrogen faces the anion.
Yes, because water molecules point the same way around any ion.

why.correct: In ion-dipole attraction, oxygen (δ−) points toward cations and hydrogen (δ+) points toward anions.
options: Like charges repel; the partly negative oxygen is attracted to the cation, not the anion.
Partly positive hydrogens are repelled by a cation. They point toward anions.
Right: opposite partial charges attract, so this is the ion-dipole orientation.
The drawing shows different orientations around the two ions, which is what makes it right.

items.q: Forming the attractions shown in the drawing has which energy effect?
options: It absorbs energy, because water has to be pulled toward the ions.
It has no energy effect, because no chemical bonds form.
It releases energy, as opposite partial charges come together.
It absorbs energy, because the ions break apart from the crystal at that moment.

why.correct: Dissolving has three steps: separating solute particles (absorbs), separating solvent particles (absorbs) and forming solute-solvent attractions (releases).
options: Attractions forming release energy; separating particles is what absorbs it.
Ion-dipole attractions are intermolecular, but forming them still releases energy.
Right: forming any attraction lowers the potential energy and releases energy (the third step of dissolving).
Separating the ions from the crystal is a different step, and that one absorbs energy.

items.q: The ion-dipole attractions in the drawing are stronger for Mg²⁺ than for Na⁺. Which is the best explanation?
options: Mg²⁺ has a larger charge and smaller radius, so its Coulombic attraction is greater.
Mg²⁺ has a larger molar mass, so it attracts water more strongly.
Mg²⁺ has more electrons than Na⁺, so it is more polarizable.
Mg²⁺ forms covalent bonds with water, while Na⁺ forms ionic bonds.

why.correct: Coulombic attraction grows with charge and falls with distance. Mg²⁺ (2+, smaller) beats Na⁺ (1+, larger).
options: Right: both the charge and the distance favor Mg²⁺.
Mass does not set the strength of an electrostatic attraction; charge and distance do.
Mg²⁺ and Na⁺ have the same number of electrons (10), and the key is charge and size.
Both form ion-dipole attractions with water; the strength differs because of charge and size.

items.q: How does the ordering of water shown in the drawing affect ΔS°soln?
options: It raises ΔS°soln, because water molecules move in closer to the ions.
It has no effect on ΔS°soln, because the water was already a liquid.
It raises ΔS°soln, because ion-dipole attractions release heat.
It lowers ΔS°soln: water held around ions has fewer arrangements.

why.correct: Hydration orders the water (S down) while the ions disperse (S up). The net sign depends on which is larger.
options: Being held close to an ion restricts the water molecules, which lowers their entropy.
The water molecules in the shells lose freedom compared with bulk liquid, so the entropy changes.
Releasing heat affects ΔH°, and through the surroundings, not the ordering effect asked about here.
Right: hydration shells reduce the freedom of the water, an entropy decrease that offsets the ions dispersing.

items.q: Which step in dissolving an ionic solid releases energy?
options: Separating the ions of the crystal from one another
Water molecules surrounding the separated ions
Separating water molecules to make room for the ions
Heating the water before the solid is added

why.correct: Separating particles absorbs energy; forming attractions releases it.
options: Pulling apart oppositely charged ions absorbs energy.
Right: forming ion-dipole attractions releases energy.
Breaking hydrogen bonds between water molecules absorbs energy.
Heating is not one of the energy steps of dissolving.

items.q: When salt Q dissolves in water, the solution warms up. Which conclusion about the steps of dissolving is supported?
options: Forming ion-dipole attractions releases more energy than separating ions and water absorbs.
Separating the ions releases more energy than forming ion-dipole attractions absorbs.
No energy is absorbed in any step, because the solution warms up.
ΔS°soln is negative, which is why the solution gets warmer.

why.correct: Warming means exothermic overall: the energy released (solute-solvent attractions) exceeds the energy absorbed (solute-solute and solvent-solvent separation).
options: Right: a warmer solution means ΔH°soln < 0, so the releasing step outweighs the absorbing steps.
This reverses the signs: separating ions absorbs energy and forming attractions releases it.
The separating steps still absorb energy; they are simply outweighed.
Temperature change tells you the sign of ΔH°, not of ΔS°.

items.q: For a salt, ΔH°soln = +15 kJ/mol and ΔS°soln = +40 J/(mol·K). How does its solubility change as the water is heated from 298 K to 373 K?
options: It decreases: ΔH°soln is positive, so heating pushes the salt out of solution.
It does not change: solubility depends on the salt, not on temperature.
It increases: TΔS° grows, so ΔG°soln falls from +3.1 to +0.1 kJ/mol.
It increases: heating makes ΔH°soln negative.

why.correct: ΔG° = 15 − T(0.040): +3.08 kJ/mol at 298 K, +0.08 kJ/mol at 373 K. Less positive ΔG° means larger K, so more salt dissolves.
options: For an endothermic dissolution, heating favors dissolving (Le Châtelier agrees).
Ksp depends on temperature through ΔG° = −RT ln K.
Right: for ΔH° > 0 and ΔS° > 0, raising T makes ΔG° less positive, so Ksp grows.
ΔH° stays about the same; it is the −TΔS° term that changes with T.

items.q: A slightly soluble salt has ΔG°soln = +30.0 kJ/mol at 298 K. Calculate its Ksp. (R = 8.314 J/(mol·K))

mistakes.why: Value: convert ΔG° to 30,000 J/mol so the units match R.

items.q: A student claims: "A salt dissolves only if dissolving releases heat." Which example disproves the claim?
options: Calcium chloride dissolving while the water warms
Ammonium nitrate dissolving while the water cools
Silver chloride barely dissolving in water
Sugar dissolving faster in hot tea than in iced tea

why.correct: Favorability depends on ΔG°, not ΔH° alone. NH₄NO₃ dissolves even though ΔH°soln > 0.
options: This fits the claim; it does not disprove it.
Right: endothermic, yet favored, because ΔS° is large enough that TΔS° > ΔH°.
A salt that barely dissolves does not test whether heat release is required.
This is about rate, not whether dissolving is favored.

items.q: Which changes would make ΔH°soln of an ionic solid more negative (more exothermic)? Select ALL that apply.
options: Stronger ion-dipole attractions between ions and water
Weaker attractions between the ions in the crystal
Stronger attractions between the ions in the crystal
A higher temperature of the water

why.correct: ΔH°soln = (energy to separate ions) + (energy to separate water) − (energy released by ion-dipole attractions). Weaker lattice or stronger hydration makes it more negative.
options: More energy released in the third step.
Less energy absorbed to separate the ions.
More energy absorbed to separate the ions: ΔH°soln becomes less negative.
ΔH°soln barely depends on temperature; the attractions decide it.
